1.pericope_label: Then Solomon began to build the house of the Lord at Jerusalem in mount Moriah, where the Lord appeared unto David his father, in the place that David had prepared in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite. And he began to build in the second day of the second month, in the fourth year of his reign. Now these are the things wherein Solomon was instructed for the building of the house of God. The length by cubits after the first measure was threescore cubits, and the breadth twenty cubits. And the porch that was in the front of the house, the length of it was according to the breadth of the house, twenty cubits, and the height was an hundred and twenty: and he overlaid it within with pure gold.

schools.summary: Ellicott does most of the textual work. He notes that nowhere else in the Old Testament is the temple site so specified, reads the clause as who appeared unto David rather than where the Lord appeared, on the strength of an etymology making Moriah the appearance of Jah, rejects the Latin rendering because the verb never means to be shown or pointed out, and traces the Syriac hill of the Amorites to a misreading of the Greek. He finds a scribe's error in the date, since the versions do not repeat in the second, and holds with Delitzsch that the next clause is not about instruction but means this is the foundation, or ground-plan, of Solomon, both taking the plural pronoun as a neuter singular and the infinitive substantively. On the hundred and twenty cubits of the porch he argues for corruption: it would make the porch four times the height of the house, the Syriac omits the clause, it has no parallel in Kings, and it wants the word cubits which the numbers here usually carry. Delitzsch sets out the order of the whole description, from the porch inwards to the most holy place and then out to the furniture of the court, and explains the ancient measure as the Mosaic cubit, a handbreadth longer than the civil cubit of later times.

Clarke supplies the Targum on the site, which has Abraham praying and worshipping there, Jacob praying there as he fled from Esau, and the angel of the Lord appearing to David. He explains why Chronicles specifies the ancient measure at all, namely that the book was written after the captivity, so that without the note a reader would assume the Babylonian cubit, a palm shorter than the cubit of Moses. On the height of the porch he suspects transposed letters, the word for a hundred being the word for a cubit with two letters exchanged, which yields twenty, agrees with the Syriac, the Arabic and the Alexandrine Greek, and brings the porch within proportion. Wesley glosses the first measure as the measure first fixed, says Solomon was instructed by David and by the Spirit of God, and alone lets the hundred and twenty cubits stand, taking the porch for a kind of turret to the building.

Henry gives five reasons why the place was fixed rather than chosen: Jerusalem, where God had put his name; Mount Moriah, which some think the very spot where Abraham offered Isaac; the place where the Lord appeared to David and answered him by fire, so that atonement having been made there once it must still be made there; the place David had prepared, not merely purchased but pitched on by divine direction, so that it was Solomon's wisdom not to enquire out a more convenient one; and a threshingfloor, whose Jebusite owner gives encouragement to the Gentiles and whose work teaches that temple-work requires the labour of the mind as threshing does that of the body. On the date he defends the three years that went before as spent in preparation rather than trifled away, and passes on a conjecture that this was a sabbatical year. From the measures he draws the lesson that the dimensions were given by divine wisdom, so that nothing can be put to them or taken away, and Solomon's first measure is his last.

5.pericope_label: And the greater house he cieled with fir tree, which he overlaid with fine gold, and set thereon palm trees and chains. And he garnished the house with precious stones for beauty: and the gold was gold of Parvaim. He overlaid also the house, the beams, the posts, and the walls thereof, and the doors thereof, with gold; and graved cherubims on the walls. And he made the most holy house, the length whereof was according to the breadth of the house, twenty cubits, and the breadth thereof twenty cubits: and he overlaid it with fine gold, amounting to six hundred talents. And the weight of the nails was fifty shekels of gold. And he overlaid the upper chambers with gold.

schools.summary: Ellicott glosses the panelling, explaining that to ciel, or rather seel, meant in old English to wainscot a room, and lines up the versions on the ornaments, the Greek giving palms and chains, the Syriac the likeness of palms and lilies, the Latin palms and as it were chainlets intertwining. He notes that the Latin explains the precious stones as a floor of costly marble, offers an auriferous region in southern Arabia for Parvaim while allowing the Sanskrit derivation that puts it in India, reads the fifty shekels as the weight of each nail on the ground that fifty as a total would be trifling beside six hundred talents, takes the upper chambers for real chambers over the holy of holies, and observes that Solomon's whole yearly revenue was six hundred and sixty-six talents. He also supplies the corroboration the others lack, that gold plating on this scale is well attested from the monuments of Nebuchadnezzar and Esarhaddon. Delitzsch calls the wood cypress, makes the ornaments artificial palms with garlands of flowers carved on the wainscot, defends the precious stones on the walls as very easily credible since Solomon brought such stones in quantity from Ophir and it was a common Eastern custom, and reports that Parvaim occurs nowhere else and has not been satisfactorily explained.

Clarke prints the Latin rendering that makes the verse describe a pavement of most precious marble, without deciding between that and the walls. On Parvaim he canvasses two identifications the others do not, that it is Sepharvaim and that it is Taprobane, now Ceylon, the name derived by Bochart from a word for border, and adds the rabbinic answer, that the gold was of a blood-red colour and took its name from the word for heifers, being like bullocks' blood. On the nails he refuses the weight outright: bolts must be intended, since it would be preposterous to suppose nails of nearly two pounds' weight. He takes the upper chambers for the ceiling. Wesley reads the nails as weighing, or rather being worth, fifty shekels, workmanship and all, and says the upper chambers are rather the roof.

Henry has the precious stones set here and there where they would show to best advantage, remarks that the finest houses now pretend to no better garnishing than good paint while these were substantially rich, and reads them as a type of the new Jerusalem, which has no temple in it because it is all temple. On the nails he agrees with Wesley that each weighed fifty shekels, or rather was worth so much, workmanship and all.

10.pericope_label: And in the most holy house he made two cherubims of image work, and overlaid them with gold. And the wings of the cherubims were twenty cubits long: one wing of the one cherub was five cubits, reaching to the wall of the house: and the other wing was likewise five cubits, reaching to the wing of the other cherub. And one wing of the other cherub was five cubits, reaching to the wall of the house: and the other wing was five cubits also, joining to the wing of the other cherub. The wings of these cherubims spread themselves forth twenty cubits: and they stood on their feet, and their faces were inward. And he made the vail of blue, and purple, and crimson, and fine linen, and wrought cherubims thereon.

schools.summary: Ellicott renders image work literally as a work of statuary, observes that the Hebrew word occurs here only and looks suspicious, and sets the versions against it, the Latin giving statuary work, the Greek a work of logs and the Syriac a durable work, the last three agreeing with the blocks of oleaster named in Kings, so that the original reading may have been simply woodwork. He translates the direction of the faces as toward the chamber and states flatly that these cherubs did not face each other as the pair on the mercy seat did. He works out the arithmetic of the wings, each five cubits so that each cherub covered ten of the chamber's twenty, the inner wings meeting in the middle and the outer touching the walls. On the veil he notes that Kings omits the curtain but does speak of the chains of gold from which it was probably suspended, and that raised figures in tapestry or broidered work are meant. Delitzsch calls the figures sculpture work from a root meaning to form or fashion, reads the repeated clauses about the wings as distributive and reaches the same arrangement, and observes that the veil is absent from the parallel while being of the same materials and colours as the veil of the tabernacle and inwoven with similar cherub figures.

Wesley takes image work in a third sense, as moveable work, not fixed to the mercy seat like the cherubim of Moses but in a moving posture, and holds with Henry that the figures were designed to represent the angels who attend the divine Majesty. On the veil he reads it as Henry does, that it denoted the darkness of that dispensation and the distance at which the worshippers were kept, but that at the death of Christ it was rent, so that through him we are brought nigh and have liberty not only to look but to enter into the holiest.

Henry explains why two more cherubim were wanted when two already stood over the ark: those were small, and continued because they were appurtenances of the ark, which alone of the tabernacle furniture was not made new, but the most holy place was now enlarged and the large pair were added, doubtless by divine appointment, to fill a room that would otherwise have looked bare and unfurnished. He puts their faces inward toward the ark and argues from it that they were not set there to be adored, since figures meant for adoration would have been made sitting, as on a throne, with their faces toward their worshippers. From this he draws the rule that we must not worship angels but must worship with angels, having come into communion with them, and that the thought of worshipping him before whom the angels cover their faces will inspire reverence in every approach to God. On the veil's cherubim he notes that the Hebrew says he caused them to ascend, which means either that they were embossed in raised work or that they were made on the wing in an ascending posture, to remind the worshippers to lift up their hearts.

15.pericope_label: Also he made before the house two pillars of thirty and five cubits high, and the chapiter that was on the top of each of them was five cubits. And he made chains, as in the oracle, and put them on the heads of the pillars; and made an hundred pomegranates, and put them on the chains. And he reared up the pillars before the temple, one on the right hand, and the other on the left; and called the name of that on the right hand Jachin, and the name of that on the left Boaz.

schools.summary: Ellicott holds that eighteen cubits is right against the thirty-five of this verse, noting that the Greek and Latin read thirty-five while the Syriac and Arabic read eighteen, and calls the chapiter the capital, literally the ornament, where Kings says the crown. On the chains he refuses the emendation most commentators have made, altering the word for the oracle into a word for collar, and changes the preposition instead, an infinitesimal change in Hebrew writing, which yields chainwork as in the chancel; he defends the sense because the chronicler has said as much of the great hall and Kings declares the whole house adorned with mural carvings, and notes that the Greek plainly had the present text and simply transliterated what it did not understand. He supplies the arithmetic that the hundred pomegranates conceal, four hundred in all on the two pillars, and ends by defending the chronicler's competence against Reuss, who called the description almost unintelligible under the pen of the abbreviator and the disputed word foreign to the text. Delitzsch also reads eighteen, accounting for thirty-five by the confusion of two similar pairs of Hebrew numeral letters, derives the word for the capital from a root meaning to overlay, emends the chains to a collar because a phrase about the most holy place has no meaning in a passage on the pillars, and describes the capital in two parts, the lower a rounded swell covered with chain-like network a cubit high and set with carved pomegranates above and below.

Clarke prints the Targum on the names, which makes Jachin commemorate the establishing of the kingdom of the house of David and derives Boaz from the patriarch of the family of Judah from whom all the kings of Judah descended, and refers the rest to the parallel in Kings. Wesley translates the two names, Jachin that he shall establish and Boaz that in it is strength.

Henry needs no emendation for the height at all, taking the thirty-five cubits and somewhat over as the measure of the two pillars together, which leaves about eighteen cubits apiece and agrees with the other accounts without touching the text. He reads the pair of names together as establishment and strength in temple-work and by it.
